translations.text: It came to pass in the eighth year of the king of the Persians that Varsken the pitiakhsh, son of Arshusha, set out for the royal court. Before this he too had been a Christian, born of a Christian father and mother.
His wife was the daughter of Vardan, commander of the Armenians, the one for whose sake I have written this to you. She was named Vardan after her father,
and her pet name was Shushanik. As we have said, she had feared God from her youth.
She was always grieved at heart by her husband's wicked ways, and she begged everyone to pray for him,
so that God might turn him from his foolish ways and he might come to the understanding of Christ.
But who could describe this wretched, thrice-pitiable and utterly lost Varsken, and how he cast away the blessed hope of Christ?
And who would not weep for him? He had faced no affliction, no fear, no sword and no imprisonment for Christ's sake!
For when he came before the king of the Persians, it was not to receive honour. Instead he offered himself as a gift to that king,
denying the true God and worshipping fire, for he cast himself away from Christ in every respect.
This pitiable man asked the king of the Persians for a wife in order to please the king, and he spoke to him like this:
"My lawful wife and my children too: I will convert them to your religion in the same way as I have converted."
He promised this even though he had no such assurance from Shushanik. Then the king rejoiced and ordered that the king's daughter be given to him as his wife.
The pitiakhsh took his leave of the king of the Persians. When he reached the borders of Kartli, in the land of Hereti, he made a plan
to send word ahead so that the nobles, his sons and his servants would come out to meet him. Through them he meant to slip into the country like a serpent.
He sent his servant ahead on a post-horse. The servant came to the town called Tsurtavi.
When he arrived and went in before Shushanik, our queen, he greeted her. But blessed Shushanik spoke to him like a prophet:
"If he is alive in spirit, then may you live, both he and you. If you are dead in spirit, may that greeting of yours come back on you!"
The man did not dare to answer her. But holy Shushanik made him swear an oath and questioned him closely.
Then the man told her the truth and said: "Varsken has denied the true God."
When blessed Shushanik heard this, she threw herself on the ground and beat her head hard, and with bitter tears she said:
"Wretched Varsken has become pitiable, for he has denied the true God, professed fire, and joined the godless."
She got up and left her palace and, in the fear of God, went into the church. She took with her her three sons and one daughter and brought them before the altar. Then she prayed like this:
"Lord God, they were given by you, so you protect them. They have been enlightened by the holy font
through the grace of the Holy Spirit, so that they may be one flock of the one shepherd, our Lord Jesus Christ!"
When they had finished the evening service, she found a small hut near the church and went into it full of bitterness. She leaned into a corner and wept bitter tears.
But the bishop of the pitiakhsh's household, whose name was Apots, was not there; he had gone to the dwelling of a certain holy man to ask about some matter.
And I too, the priest of Queen Shushanik, was with that bishop.
At once a deacon came to us from home and told us all this: the arrival of the pitiakhsh and what the queen had done.
We were filled with grief and wept with great weeping, distressed that our sins had been revealed.
I set out early and reached the village where the blessed Shushanik was.
When I saw her in distress, I wept with her too. And I said to the blessed Shushanik: "You are about to enter a great contest, my queen!
Guard the faith of Christ, so that the enemy, like a moth, does not find pasture in you."
The holy Shushanik said to me: "Priest, I am indeed ready for a great contest." And I said to her: "So it is.
Be brave, patient and long-suffering." But she said to me: "These troubles are mine alone!"
I said to her: "Your troubles are our troubles, and your joy is our joy.
You were not only our queen; you looked after all of us as your children."
And I said to the blessed woman: "Tell me in confidence [?] what you intend, so that I may know it and write down your struggle."
She said to me: "Why do you ask me this?" I answered her: "Do you stand firm?" And she said to me:
"Far be it from me to share in the deeds and sins of Varsken!" I answered her: "He has a cruel mind. He will subject you to beatings and great torment."
She said to me: "It is better for me to die at his hands than to be united with him again and lose my soul,
for I have heard from the Apostle Paul: 'A brother or a sister is not bound; let them separate.'" And I said: "So it is."
While we were talking about this, a Persian man came and went in to the blessed Shushanik. Weeping, he said:
"How has such a peaceful house become so pitiable, and joy turned to grief!"
But he was acting on Varsken's plan. He said this deceitfully and wanted to trap the blessed woman.
The saint recognized his deceitful intent and guarded herself firmly.
Three days later Varsken the pitiakhsh arrived. The Persian spoke to him in secret and said: "From what I have learned, your wife has separated from you.
And I tell you: do not say anything harsh to her, for women's nature is weak."
The next day, when the pitiakhsh got up, he called for us priests, and we went. He greeted us gladly and said to us:
"Now you need not be shy of me at all, and I no longer hate you." We answered him: "You have destroyed yourself, and you have destroyed us too."
Only then did he begin to speak, and he said: "How did my wife dare to do such a thing to me?
Now go and say to her: 'You have overturned my image and poured ashes on my bed.
And you have abandoned your place and gone off elsewhere.'" But holy Shushanik said: "Was it I who set up that image? Then I might have overturned it!
Your father set up martyrs' shrines and built churches, but you have undone your father's works and turned his good deeds into something else.
Your father brought saints into his house, but you have brought in demons. He confessed and believed in the God of heaven and earth,
but you have denied the true God and bow down to fire. And just as you have denied your Creator, so I too have scorned you.
And even if you bring many tortures on me, I will have no part in your deeds!"
We reported all this to the pitiakhsh. He grew angry at heart and raged against her.
Then he sent Jojik, his brother, and Jojik's wife, his sister-in-law, and the bishop of his household, and said to them:
"Tell her this: 'Get up and come back to your place, and do not keep such a mind. Otherwise I will drag you here by force!'"
When they arrived, they went in before the queen and spoke many persuasive words to her. Then holy Shushanik said to them:
"Wise men, you speak well, but do not believe that I would still be a wife to him.
I thought that I would turn him to my faith and he would confess the true God. And now you compel me to do this?! May this never happen to me!
And you, Jojik, are no longer my brother-in-law, nor am I your sister-in-law, nor is your wife my sister, since you are on his side and share in his deeds."
Jojik said to her: "Know this: now they will send servants, and he will have you dragged away by force."
But holy Shushanik said: "If he binds me and drags me, I will rejoice, for in that way my separation from him will be settled."
When they heard this from her, they all wept, and Jojik got up and went outside in tears. And holy Shushanik said to the bishop:
"How can you tell me to give in, when he has denied God?!" But Jojik pleaded with her and said: "You are our sister. Do not destroy this royal house."
Holy Shushanik said to him: "I know that I am your sister and that we were brought up together, but I cannot do that, even if it should come to bloodshed and all of you be held guilty."
And as they pressed her hard, the holy and blessed Shushanik rose and took her Gospel with her, and weeping she said this:
"Lord God, you know that I go willingly to death."
She said this and went with them, and she took with her her Gospel and the holy books of the martyrs.
When she entered the palace, she did not sit in her own upper chamber, but in a small cell.
Holy Shushanik lifted her hands to heaven and said: "Lord God, not even among the priests was anyone merciful found,
nor did any layman stand out among this people. Instead, all of them have handed me over to death, to Varsken, the enemy of God."
Two days later the wolf came to the palace and said to his servants:
"When Jojik, his wife and I eat bread together, let no one else be allowed to come in with us."
And when evening came, they summoned Jojik's wife and decided to eat together, so that they might bring in holy Shushanik as well.
And when the time for the meal came, Jojik and his wife went in to holy Shushanik so that they might get her to eat bread too, for she had spent all those days fasting.
And after they pressed her hard and brought her to the palace with difficulty, she still tasted nothing.
Then Jojik's wife offered her wine in a cup and urged her to drink at least that. Holy Shushanik said to her in anger:
"When has it ever happened until now that men and women ate bread together?!" And she thrust out her hand, dashed the cup into her face and spilled the wine.
Then Varsken began to revile her shamefully and trampled her with his feet. He took a poker and struck her on the head, gashing it, and he made one of her eyes swell up.
And he struck her in the face with his fist without mercy and dragged her back and forth by the hair. Like a raging wild beast he shouted and bellowed, like a madman.
Then Jojik, his brother, rose up to intervene, and they struggled until Jojik too was beaten and struck on the head. With difficulty, like a lamb from a wolf, he got her out of his hands.
And holy Shushanik lay on the ground like a dead woman, while Varsken cursed her family and lineage and called her the destroyer of the house.
And he ordered that she be bound and that fetters be put on her feet.
And when his rage had calmed a little, the Persian came and earnestly begged him to release holy Shushanik from her bonds.
And because he begged so much, Varsken ordered that she be released, brought into a cell, and carefully guarded by a single servant,
and that no one else should go in to see her, neither man nor woman.
And as soon as it was dawn, he asked her servant: "How is she after her wounds?" And the servant said to him:
"She cannot recover." Then he went in himself and saw her, and he was astonished at how badly she was swollen.
And he gave the servant orders, saying: "Let no one go in to see her." And he himself went off hunting.
But I got up, went, and said to the guard: "Let me go in, just me alone, and see her wounds."
But he said to me: "What if he finds out and kills me?" And I said to him: "You wretch, were you not raised by her? And if he kills you for her sake, what of it?" Then he let me in secretly.
And when I went inside, I saw her face, cracked open and swollen, and I cried out aloud and wept.
But holy Shushanik said to me: "Do not weep for me, for this night has become the beginning of joy for me." And I said to holy Shushanik: "Allow me to
wash the blood from your face and the ashes that have been driven into your eyes, and to put salve and medicine on you, so that perhaps you may be healed."
But holy Shushanik said to me: "Priest, do not say that, for this blood cleanses my sins."
Then I urged her a little to take the food that Bishop Samuel and John had sent, for they were secretly looking after her and comforting her.
Then holy Shushanik said to me: "Priest, I cannot taste anything, for my jaws and some of my teeth are crushed."
Then I took a little wine and soaked some bread, and she tasted a little. And I hurried to leave.

Then holy Shushanik said to me: "Priest, shouldn't I send him this jewelry of his? He may ask for it, because I have no more need of it in this life!" But I said: "Don't be in any hurry; let it stay with you."
While we were still talking this over, a boy came and said: "Is Jacob there?" I said: "What do you want?" And he said to me: "The pitiakhsh is summoning you."
I was surprised and wondered why he was summoning me at this hour. I hurried and went, and he said to me: "Do you know, priest, that I am going off to war against the Huns?
I will not leave my jewelry with her. Since she is no longer my wife, someone will be found who will [?] it.
Go and bring me all of it, whatever there is!" So I went and told holy Shushanik.
She rejoiced greatly, gave thanks to God, and sent me everything.
I brought it to the pitiakhsh, and he took it from me, looked it over, and found it all there. And he said again: "Someone else will yet be found who will be adorned with this."
When the Great Fast arrived, the blessed Shushanik went to a place near the holy church, looked for a small cell, and shut herself up there.
The cell had a small window, and she blocked it up. She stayed in that darkness, fasting, praying and weeping.
One of the pitiakhsh's own people said to him: "Do not strike her at all during these holy fasts."
When the Monday of the Completion arrived and the pitiakhsh came back from the war against the Huns, the devil was digging at his heart.
He got up, went to the church, and said to Bishop Apots: "Give me back my wife! Why are you separating her from me?" And he began to curse and to blaspheme
God savagely. But one priest said to him: "Lord, why are you acting like this, speaking such evil, insulting the bishop,
and speaking to holy Shushanik in anger?" But he struck that priest on the back with a staff, and the priest did not dare to speak any more.
And so he dragged holy Shushanik through the mud and over thorns, all the way from the church to the palace, dragging her like a dead woman; and in places brambles had been spread on the ground.
He himself kept planting his feet on those brambles, and Shushanik's [?] and flesh were torn to shreds by the brambles. And in this way they brought her into the palace.
He ordered her to be bound and beaten. He abused her, saying: "There, look! Your church has not helped you, nor have those Christians of yours who back you, nor their Lord!"
When they had struck her about three hundred times with the rod, no cry of pain burst from her mouth, not even a groan.
Then holy Shushanik said to the lawless Varsken: "Wretch, you had no mercy even on yourself and have fallen away from God; would you have mercy on me?!"
When he saw the great quantity of blood running down her tender flesh, he ordered a chain to be put on her neck.
He ordered one of his chamberlains to have holy Shushanik taken to the fortress and shut in a dark prison, so that she would die there.
A deacon of that bishop was standing beside holy Shushanik at the moment when they were leading her out of the palace, and he wanted to say to her:
"Stand firm!" But the pitiakhsh fixed his eyes on him, and he could say nothing more. He only said to her: "Stand fi...", then fell silent and started to run away in haste.
Then they brought her out, and holy Shushanik was led along barefoot and with her hair let down, like one of the despised,
and no one dared to cover her head, for the pitiakhsh followed close behind her on horseback and reviled her with many insults.
And a great crowd of women and men went along with the saint, a countless multitude, for they followed behind her;
they raised their voices and wept, and tore their cheeks, and pitifully shed their tears for holy Shushanik.
But holy Shushanik looked back at the people and said to them: "Do not weep, my brothers and my sisters and my children, but remember me in your prayers.
And I shall be parted from you from now on, for you will no longer see me come out of the fortress alive."
And when the pitiakhsh saw that crowd and the weeping of men and women, of old and young, he chased them this way and that on horseback and put them all to flight.
And when they reached the bridge of the fortress, the pitiakhsh said to holy Shushanik:
"This much walking on your own feet is all that is left for you, for you will no longer come out alive, unless four men carry you out."
And when they entered the fortress, they found a small room on the north side, small and dark, and there they put the saint.
And the chain that had been put on her neck stayed on her as before, and the lawless Varsken sealed it with his own seal.
But holy Shushanik said: "I rejoice in this, that I may suffer here and find rest there." And the pitiakhsh said to her: "Yes, yes, rest!"
Then he set guards over her and ordered them to kill her by starvation.
And he spoke to them thus: "I tell you, if anyone goes in to her, man or woman, look to yourselves and your wives and children and houses!
I will be blameless for whatever I do to you!" Then he went out of the fortress.
And on the third Sunday he summoned one of the guards and questioned him, saying: "Is that wretched woman still alive by now?" And he said:
"Lord, she seems closer to death than to life, for she is dying, mostly of hunger, since she takes no food at all."
And he said: "Do not pity her at all; leave her be, let her die!"
But I spoke to that guard with many entreaties and promised him a drinking vessel.
And only reluctantly did he agree to let me in, and he said to me: "When it grows dark, come, but only alone."
And when the guard brought me in and I saw that lamb of Christ, beautiful as a bride, adorned with those fetters, my heart could not bear it, and I wept greatly.
But holy Shushanik said to me: "Do you weep over this good thing, priest?" And the guard said to me: "Had I known this, I would not have let you in."
But I began to speak to her and strengthen her, as far as God gave me words to speak. And I parted from her and went quickly to my own dwelling.
And the pitiakhsh set out for Chor. And Jojik, his brother, had not been present when this was done to holy Shushanik. And when Jojik arrived, he went after the pitiakhsh.
And he caught up with him at the borders of Hereti, and begged him earnestly to order that she be released from her fetters.
And as he was greatly grieved, he ordered that she be released only from the bonds.
And when Jojik came, he removed the chain from her neck. But the holy Shushanik would not consent to [the removal of] the fetters, and kept them on until her death.
For she spent six years in that fortress, and she lived by a godly rule:
with constant fasting, with vigils, with standing [in prayer], with prostrations without weariness, and with untiring reading of books.
She made that whole fortress bright and beautiful with that spiritual harp.
And from then on her deeds became known throughout all Kartli. And men and women came to offer their vows, and whatever anyone needed
was granted through the holy prayer of the blessed Shushanik, which God, the lover of mankind, granted to her: children to the childless, healing to the sick, sight to the blind.
There was a certain woman, a Persian magian, who suffered from the disease of leprosy.
And she came to the holy Shushanik, and Shushanik taught her to give up her magian religion and become a Christian. And the woman quickly agreed.
And she instructed the woman and said to her: "Go to Jerusalem, and you will be cleansed of your leprosy."
And the woman eagerly accepted this and set out on the road in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. And she was healed of her disease.
And when she returned with great joy and arrived back there, she came to the holy Shushanik to give thanks, and went to her own home rejoicing and healed.
And the holy Shushanik, instead of embroidery work, took up the Psalms with great zeal, and after a few days she had learned all one hundred and fifty psalms,
with which, day and night, with tears, she offered that pleasing hymn to the King on high.
And they told the blessed Shushanik: "He has converted your children to the magian religion."
Then she began to bow down to God with great weeping, and she struck her head on the ground, sighed, and said: "I thank you, O Lord my God, for
they were never mine; they were given by you. As you wish, let your will be done, O Lord, and protect me from the works of the enemy."
And I went and saw the holy Shushanik, wasted away and swollen from weeping.
And the holy bishop had sent her food, and when I pressed her hard, she tasted only a little of it, and we gave thanks to God.
And until that time her children used to come to see their mother. But once they had turned and had even denied God, they no longer dared to see her; they even hated to hear her name.

And afterward the pitiakhsh sent messengers and said to her: "Either do my will and come to the palace, or, if you will not come home, I will hand you over to Chor, or to the [royal] court, under guard."

But the holy Shushanik answered him thus: "O wretched and senseless man, if you send me to the court, do not send me to Chor. Who knows whether I may meet with something good there and escape this evil."
And the pitiakhsh pondered in his heart over those words that she had said to him:
"Who knows whether I may meet with something good" — [thinking] that perhaps she might become the wife of one of the princes. And from then on he sent no one to her any more.
But the holy Shushanik had said this with regard to enduring those cruel torments, so that she might please God.
Then the pitiakhsh chose her own milk-brother to bring her to the palace.
When that man said to her, "Listen to me and come down to the palace, and do not ruin that house of yours," holy Shushanik said to him:
"Say to that godless man: 'You struck me and said to me, "You will not come out of that fortress alive, on your own feet."'
Now, if you are able to raise the dead, first raise your mother, who is buried at Urdi.
But if you cannot raise her, neither can you bring me out, unless you drag me out by force."
When he reported those words to the pitiakhsh, the pitiakhsh said, "I truly did say that."
On the next day someone came in and said to holy Shushanik:
"You answered him well with that word, because he intended to lure you out in that way, and he had devised in his heart another evil plan against you."
Holy Shushanik said to him: "And do not think that God is asleep, who prepares the words in a person's mouth.
For the Lord himself says: 'I will give the answer in your place.'"
As the sixth year in that prison was coming to an end, [?] (jekma) the exhaustion from the labours of her endurance brought a sickness upon her.
I had warned her about this in advance and told her: "Do not, [?] (jekma), for you are putting too heavy a burden on that body of yours.
It will not hold out for you, and afterwards you will not be able to do any good work at all, with such severe fasting, constant standing, and toiling all night long with psalms and hymns."
Yet she did not give her body even a little rest anywhere, and it wasted away and melted like ash [?].
During the great forty-day fasts, until they were completed, in those six years she would not sit down by day or by night.
She would not sleep or take any food, except that on Sunday she received the body and blood of Christ our God.
She would take only a little broth made of pears, and only a little of that, and she did not taste bread until the fast was over.
From the day they imprisoned her in that fortress, she did not lay her head on a cushion. Instead she used a single small mud brick as her pillow.
For bedding she had one small old rug [?]. To deceive people's eyes, she had placed a small cushion of felt [?] at the pillow end.
For making her prostrations, one small haircloth was spread on the ground before her. Fleas and lice beyond imagining were crawling all over that place.
In summer there was the fiery burning and heat of the sun, scorching winds and harmful waters. The inhabitants of that place were also full of disease:
swollen with dropsy and jaundiced, spotted [?], parched [?] and [?], scrofulous [?], swollen-faced and short-lived. There is no old person in those lands.
For six years she was imprisoned in such a fortress, and in those heavy fetters she glorified God.
As the seventh year began, sores also broke out on the body of the holy and thrice-blessed Shushanik.
Because of her ceaseless labours her feet swelled, and pus [?] came out of them in place after place.
The wounds were very large, and worms had gathered in them. She picked them up with her own hand and showed them to me, and she gave thanks to God and said:
"Priest, do not let this grieve you, for the worm there is greater and does not die."
When I saw the worms I was grieved beyond imagining and wept bitterly. Again she spoke to me angrily:
"Priest, why are you grieved? Rather than be eaten by those immortal worms, it is better to be eaten by these mortal ones here, in this life."
I answered her: "Did the haircloth garment seem too small a torment to you? And now you rejoice over these worms!" She rebuked me and said:
"Tell no one about the haircloth garment while I am alive, for soon I am to leave this wretched flesh of mine."
For underneath she wore haircloth, and no one knew of it but me, while outwardly, before people's eyes, she wore an Antiochene cloak (palekarti) [?].
When Jojik heard that the blessed queen, holy Shushanik, was near death,
he went, taking with him his wife, his children, and his menservants and maidservants, and came to the fortress to see the blessed martyr Shushanik.
When he arrived, he got in only with difficulty. He bowed before the precious cross and greeted holy Shushanik. He sat down beside her and asked her about her sufferings.
The saint said to him: "I am well, as God wills, but I too am going on the road that everyone must travel."
Jojik quickly stood up and confessed to her his earlier lawless deeds. He pleaded with holy Shushanik and said to her:
"Daughter-in-law and handmaid of Christ, ask God to forgive me my many sins."
Holy Shushanik said to him: "If you do nothing else of that kind, childishly, God will forgive you."
Jojik said: "That is the very reason I have come to you, so that I will not do anything that is not pleasing to God."
Holy Shushanik said: "If you do so, you will make me immortal by that word, and may God add to the days of your life."
Then, when Jojik perceived that the saint would depart from this flesh that day, he said:
"Bless me, and my wife, your handmaid, and my children, and my menservants and maidservants.
And if we have sinned against you in anything, as people of this passing life and lovers of the world, forgive us and do not remember our insolence."
Holy Shushanik said to Jojik and his wife: "Make haste in this matter of ours, for no one was found among men
who had mercy and felt pain for me, who would have admonished that godless husband of this passing world."
They said to her: "We strove hard on your behalf without your knowing, but he would neither listen nor answer."
Then holy Shushanik said: "Let me and Varsken the pitiakhsh be judged there, where there is no partiality before the Judge of judges and King of kings,
where no distinction is made between man and woman, where he and I shall speak as equals before our God Jesus Christ.
May the Lord repay him, for he plucked my fruits before their time, put out my lamp, withered my flower, darkened the beauty of my goodness, and brought my glory low.
May God judge between him and me. But I now thank God for this,
that through his torments I shall find joy, and for his beatings and draggings I shall attain rest, and for his heartlessness and mercilessness I await mercy from Jesus Christ, my Lord."
And at all these words of hers they wept bitterly and said to her:
"Forgive us our faults and bless us, holy witness and blessed martyr of Christ God."
And holy Shushanik said to them: "May God forgive you for what you have done."
Then she blessed Jojik and his wife and his children and his servants and maidservants, and all his household and his palace.
And she urged them to walk in the ways of God and said to them: "All this life is like the flower of the fields: it passes away and does not last. Whoever has sown will reap,
and whoever has scattered to the poor has gathered; and whoever loses his own life will find it, the one who has glorified Him." And she bade them farewell and sent them away in peace.
Then after Jojik came Samuel, the head of the bishops, and Bishop John, his companion. They had strengthened her and been very zealous for her;

together with their households they had been with her, they had been her servants and sharers and partakers in her labours, and now with thanksgiving they were sending her off toward that harbour of Christ.
In the same way the great nobles and high-born ladies, nobles and commoners of the land of Kartli, came likewise,
those who had zealously shared in her labours, and with blessings they committed her to Christ as a valiant champion.
And all those bishops and nobles together made one request of her:
that she would grant the fetter from her feet as a [?] and a blessing for all. To this holy Shushanik said to them: "What am I, unworthy as I am?
But because of your love for God, may the priest fulfil your wish concerning that thing. For what am I able to do?
But may Christ, who is all-full, fill you with every good thing, you who have toiled for me and shared in these my sufferings and afflictions and torments.
And I, beloved ones, behold, I am now going on my road to eternity, which has been prepared for me beforehand.
In place of this affliction of mine may Christ grant me joy, and in place of these torments, rest;
and for these beatings and draggings and insults of mine may I attain glory and unending honour in heaven."
And they, having taken their leave, full of tears, offered glory to God for her victory. And they came out of the fortress and went away.
And the day of her calling came, and she summoned Aphots, the bishop of her house, and gave him thanks for his loving care toward her:
"Like a father and a foster-father, you have received [?] me, this sinful and poor person."
And she entrusted to him the remains of her bones and commanded that they be laid in the place from which she had first been dragged out, and she said to him:
"If I, this last worker of the vineyard, who came at the eleventh hour, am worthy of anything, may all of you be blessed to the ages of ages."
And she gave thanks to God and said: "Blessed is the Lord my God, for in peace I lie down upon it and sleep."
And she commended her soul to the Lord, who receives all.
And then at once the blessed bishop John brought a cloth [?] to wrap the holy of holies, her precious relics.
And so the rest of us lifted up the body, which was badly withered and eaten by worms. We washed off the earthy worms and the rot [?], and clothed it in that cloth.

And then the two bishops, John and Apots, and we with them, like strong oxen under a spiritual yoke, with lit candles and fragrant incense, took up the precious bones and carried them out to the holy church.
And we laid the holy, glorious and honored relics of Saint Shushanik to rest in the place that had been prepared.
And that night we kept vigil all night like angels, and with the harp of David we glorified almighty God and his Son, our Lord
Jesus Christ, who has power over all things for all people, and gives courage to fathers and mothers alike,
and grants to his own the victory of his power, to all who seek him with one heart.
The torments of Saint Shushanik began on the eighth day of the month of Apni, on a Wednesday;

her second beating came on a Monday, after the eve of the Easter fast; her torture came again on the nineteenth of the month of Vardoba; and her death came on the seventeenth of the month of Ikdonberi (October),
the feast day of the holy and blessed martyrs Cosmas and Damian.
And it was a Thursday, the day on which we established the commemoration of Saint Shushanik, to the glory and praise of God,
the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, to whom glory is due forever and ever. Amen.
